question.ans: Four rungs. Côtes du Rhône, the regional appellation covering both north and south, at about 51 hl/ha. Côtes du Rhône Villages at 44. Côtes du Rhône Villages with a named commune — some twenty-odd villages including Plan de Dieu, Sablet, Séguret, Laudun, Chusclan — at 41. Then the crus, which drop the Côtes du Rhône name entirely and sit between roughly 35 and 40 hl/ha: Châteauneuf-du-Pape at 35, Gigondas at 36, the northern crus nearer 40. Yield falls at every step, along with permitted vigour and, in the crus, the right to certain varieties or colours. A named village that performs gets promoted — Vinsobres in 2006, Rasteau's dry reds in 2010, Cairanne in 2016.
question.exp: Candidates routinely skip the named-commune rung, which is the one the examiner is listening for. Note also what the ladder is not: a cru is a separate appellation, not a grade of Côtes du Rhône, so declassified cru fruit falls to Côtes du Rhône rather than stepping down one rung to Villages.

Simonsberg-Stellenbosch: north-eastern, decomposed-granite slopes facing the mountain, the district's Cabernet and Pinotage heartland — Kanonkop, Rustenberg, Thelema. question.q: Name the Muscat vins doux naturels of the Languedoc, Roussillon and Corsica, say which Muscat each may use, and explain mutage.
accept: frontignan mireval lunel saint-jean-de-minervois and rivesaltes, muscat blanc a petits grains except rivesaltes which may add alexandria
muscat blanc a petits grains for all but rivesaltes, mutage is fortifying the fermenting must with neutral spirit
frontignan lunel mireval st jean de minervois rivesaltes cap corse, spirit added during fermentation to keep sugar
mutage adds grape spirit mid-ferment, up to 10 percent of volume, leaving 100 grams of sugar
question.ans: In the Languedoc: Muscat de Frontignan, Muscat de Mireval, Muscat de Lunel and Muscat de Saint-Jean-de-Minervois, all 100% Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains. In Roussillon: Muscat de Rivesaltes, the only one that may blend Petits Grains with Muscat of Alexandria. Corsica adds Muscat du Cap Corse, again Petits Grains. Mutage is the fortification step: neutral grape spirit of around 96% is run into the fermenting must, killing the yeast and leaving the grape's own sugar unfermented. The spirit must fall between 5% and 10% of the volume; the wines finish at roughly 15–18% alcohol with at least 100 g/l of residual sugar, and the best Muscats are bottled early and protectively to keep the grape aroma.
question.exp: Two distinctions win the point. First, vin doux naturel is fortified during fermentation (like Port) whereas vin de liqueur — Pineau des Charentes, Floc de Gascogne, Macvin — is fortified before it starts. Second, the Muscats are made reductively for freshness while the Grenache-based VDN of Banyuls, Maury and Rivesaltes are the oxidative, rancio side of the same law. A candidate who adds Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise is correct — same VDN law, same Petits Grains, but in the southern Rhône rather than the Midi. The technique is credited to Arnau de Vilanova at Montpellier in the thirteenth century.
